title: “HUSBANDS, STOP HURTING THE WOMAN YOU SAY YOU LOVE.”
paragraphs: “HUSBANDS, STOP HURTING THE WOMAN YOU SAY YOU LOVE.”
Colossians 3:19 contains only a handful of words—but one of them confronts a kind of marital cruelty that can hide behind closed doors, Christian language, and even a man’s claim to “lead” his home.
There is a kind of pain nobody sees on Sunday morning.
She walks into church beside him.
She smiles.
He shakes hands.
They sit together.
They may even open the same Bible.
Nobody knows what happened in the car.
Nobody heard his tone last night.

Nobody saw her standing silently in the kitchen after another cutting remark, wondering how the man who once promised to cherish her became the person whose footsteps make her emotionally brace herself.
There may be no bruise anyone can photograph.
No shattered furniture.
No police report.
Just words.
Coldness.
Contempt.
Mockery.
Constant criticism.
A temper everyone in the house has learned to navigate.
A wife slowly discovering that silence sometimes feels safer than honesty.
And then, sitting quietly in Scripture, comes a command so direct that a husband cannot honestly read it and pretend God has nothing to say about how he treats his wife:
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.”
—Colossians 3:19, KJV
The Greek is even more revealing:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας καὶ μὴ πικραίνεσθε πρὸς αὐτάς.
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas kai mē pikrainesthe pros autas.
“Husbands, love your wives, and do not be embittered toward them.”
That word matters.
πικραίνεσθε — pikrainesthe.
It comes from language associated with becoming bitter, embittered, irritated, or harsh.
Paul does not merely tell a husband what he must do.
He confronts what he must refuse to become.
Because sometimes the destruction of a marriage does not begin when a husband stops saying, “I love you.”
Sometimes it begins when his love becomes mixed with bitterness.
When tenderness becomes irritation.
When correction becomes humiliation.
When leadership becomes control.
When disagreement becomes punishment.
When silence becomes a weapon.
When sarcasm becomes normal.
When she has to study his face before deciding whether it is safe to speak.
And a man can call himself a Christian while slowly becoming harsh toward the very woman God commanded him to love.
Read the verse again.
“Husbands, love your wives…”
The command is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate, from ἀγαπάω — agapaō.
This is not merely romantic emotion.
Biblical love is not reduced to butterflies, chemistry, attraction, or the feeling a man had when he first pursued her.
This love acts.
This love gives.
This love seeks another person’s good.
This love refuses to make selfishness its master.
And the New Testament gives husbands an even more staggering picture of what marital love should resemble.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Read that slowly.
Not:
“Husbands, make sure she knows who is boss.”
Not:
“Husbands, win every argument.”
Not:
“Husbands, demand respect while refusing tenderness.”
Not:
“Husbands, use Scripture to make your wife afraid of disagreeing with you.”
Christ.
Loved.
The church.
And gave Himself.
The model placed before a Christian husband is a crucified Savior.
That changes everything.
Jesus did not demonstrate His authority by selfishly crushing His bride.
He gave Himself for her.
So whenever biblical headship is twisted into permission for intimidation, degradation, coercion, selfish domination, or cruelty, something has gone terribly wrong.
The cross does not give a husband permission to become a tyrant.
The cross calls him to die to himself.
And maybe that sentence hurts.
Maybe you are the husband reading this and remembering things you said that you wish you could pull back out of the air.
Maybe you remember her face changing after you said them.
Maybe you knew exactly where she was vulnerable…
and you aimed there anyway.
Maybe afterward you justified it.
“She started it.”
“She knows how to push my buttons.”
“She should respect me.”
“I was angry.”
“She needed to hear the truth.”
But truth does not need cruelty to become true.
And anger does not magically turn sin into righteousness.
Scripture says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”
—James 1:19–20, KJV
Your anger is not automatically God’s anger.
Your volume is not spiritual authority.
Winning an argument is not the same as loving your wife.
Being the husband does not make every reaction righteous.
And saying “I provide for this family” cannot purchase permission to wound the people living inside it.
You can pay every bill and still leave an emotional debt your wife has been carrying for years.
You can put food on the table while starving a marriage of tenderness.
You can protect your house from strangers while making your own family afraid of your temper.
You can know theology and still fail to sound like Jesus when you are angry.
That is what makes Colossians 3:19 so uncomfortable.
God does not merely care whether a marriage remains legally intact.
He cares about what kind of man a husband is becoming inside that marriage.
But husbands are not the only people who need to hear this.
Some wife reading this has spent years wondering whether she is simply “too sensitive.”
Someone repeatedly told you that his cruelty was your fault.
Perhaps every confrontation somehow ended with you apologizing.
Perhaps Scripture itself was thrown at you whenever you tried to describe what was hurting you.
Hear this carefully:
Colossians 3:19 exists because God cares how a husband treats his wife.
Christian marriage is never a biblical excuse for abuse.
A command to love cannot honestly be transformed into permission to terrorize.
And forgiveness does not require pretending evil never happened.
Reconciliation and restored trust are not produced by demanding that an injured person immediately behave as though nothing occurred. Genuine repentance bears fruit.
John the Baptist said:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
—Matthew 3:8, KJV
Real repentance is more than:
“Fine. Sorry.”
It is more than tears after consequences arrive.
It is more than flowers after another explosion.
It is more than quoting Scripture when your marriage begins falling apart.
Repentance turns.
Repentance confesses.
Repentance stops defending what God is confronting.
Repentance seeks forgiveness without demanding immediate restoration of trust.
Repentance accepts accountability.
Repentance asks, “How have I wounded you?” and develops enough humility to listen to the answer.

And when patterns involve abuse, threats, violence, coercion, or genuine danger, seeking appropriate outside help and immediate safety is not rebellion against biblical marriage. No person should be pressured to remain in immediate danger simply to preserve appearances.
But there is another husband reading this.
You are not hitting your wife.
You do not threaten her.
You would never describe yourself as abusive.
Yet something inside you knows the Holy Spirit is pressing on an area you have tried not to examine.
The eye rolls.
The dismissive sigh.
The way you speak to her as though she is stupid.
The jokes at her expense.
The constant corrections.
The affection you withhold when she disappoints you.
The days of cold silence.
The comparison to another woman.
The phone receiving more of your attention than your wife.
The apology you refuse to give because your pride cannot survive three words:
I was wrong.
Brother…
what if your marriage does not primarily need you to prove that you are right?
What if it needs you to become more like Christ?
There was a time when you looked at this woman and thanked God she chose you.
You waited for her messages.
You wanted another hour with her.
You noticed things.
You listened.
You were gentle.

Somewhere between courtship and mortgages, children, exhaustion, disappointments, responsibilities, unanswered expectations, and accumulated wounds, familiarity may have turned something precious into something you began taking for granted.
Now imagine losing what you stopped appreciating.
Imagine the empty chair.
The silent room.
The photographs.
The memories.
The realization that there were a thousand ordinary evenings when you could have reached across the distance and said:
“Come here.”
“I’m listening.”
“I’m sorry.”
“Forgive me.”
“I still choose you.”
Do not wait for a funeral to become tender.
Do not wait for separation to become attentive.
Do not wait until her heart has spent years bleeding before deciding her pain matters.
Love her now.
Not because she is flawless.
She isn't.
Neither are you.
Love her because Jesus is teaching you how redeemed men love.
And that is where this becomes Gospel.
Because Colossians 3:19 is not merely another rule for men who need to try harder.
The entire Christian life collapses if all we have is human willpower.
We need Christ.
We need the Savior who does not merely expose sin but saves sinners.
We need the Jesus who walked toward a cross carrying the judgment our sin deserved.
We need grace.
Because some husbands will read this and feel conviction.
Good.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction says:
Bring it into the light.
Condemnation whispers:
Hide. You are beyond redemption.
The Gospel says something far more powerful.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Not excuse.
Not minimize.
Not rename.
Confess.
There is mercy at the feet of Jesus for the husband finally willing to tell the truth.
There is grace for the proud man who becomes humble.
There is forgiveness for the man who has failed.
There is transformation for the man who stops asking Jesus merely to improve his marriage and begins asking Jesus to transform him.
Maybe tonight your first act of leadership should not be another lecture.
Maybe it should be repentance.
Put the phone down.
Look at your wife.
Do not explain yourself first.
Do not tell her what she did wrong.
Do not attach “but” to your apology.
Tell the truth.
“I have been harsh with you.”
“I have not loved you the way Christ calls me to love you.”
“I have hurt you.”
“I am sorry.”
“Will you forgive me?”
Then understand something important:
She may cry.
She may not immediately believe you.
She may have heard apologies before.
Do not punish her for needing time.
Become the apology.
Let repentance become visible in the way you speak tomorrow.
And next week.
And six months from now.
Let the Gospel reach your tone.
Your temper.
Your jokes.
Your disagreements.
Your spending.
Your sexuality.
Your attention.
Your phone.
Your priorities.
Your pride.
Your private behavior.
Your treatment of the woman you vowed to love.
Because Christianity that transforms a man at church but never reaches the way he speaks to his wife at home has left one of the most important rooms of his discipleship untouched.
And wife…
if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you wish your husband understood these words, Jesus sees you.
Your worth is not determined by another human being’s inability to recognize it.
You were not created merely to absorb someone else’s bitterness.
Bring your pain to Christ, and where serious harm is occurring, bring it into the light with trustworthy, mature help rather than carrying it entirely alone.
And to every unmarried man reading this:
Do not wait until marriage to learn gentleness.
The wedding ring will not crucify your ego for you.
Become now the kind of man who can hear correction without exploding.
Become now the kind of man who can apologize without manipulating.
Become now the kind of man whose strength makes people feel protected rather than intimidated.
Follow Jesus now.
Because someday somebody may place her heart frighteningly close to yours.
Handle it like something God can see.
And He can.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want Scripture to enter the places people hide.
The marriage nobody knows is hurting.
The believer quietly drifting.
The husband fighting pride.
The wife needing biblical encouragement.
The Christian who has learned church language but desperately needs Jesus to invade ordinary life again.
If this article exposed something in you, do not rush past the conviction.
Sit with God.
Pray.
Open Colossians 3 again.
And if necessary, go find the person you wounded.
Be honest.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your pain. But sometimes three honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not fighting alone.
You may never know whose marriage is sitting one conversation away from repentance.
It does not purchase a blessing.
It does not replace obedience to Christ, generosity toward people in need, or faithful giving according to your conscience and biblical convictions.
Christian giving is not supposed to be extracted by spiritual pressure.
Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That is exactly why support should come freely.
Pray.
Share truth.
Live the Gospel.
Send this to someone who needs it.
It would be another heart surrendered to Christ.
Another husband repenting.
Another wife being treated with Christlike tenderness.

Another family discovering that the Gospel is not merely something we believe on Sunday—it is something Jesus intends to carry into the kitchen, the bedroom, the argument, the apology, and every ordinary moment behind the closed doors nobody else sees.
Maybe your story contains chapters you are ashamed of.
Maybe your marriage does too.
Words you cannot retrieve.
Nights you cannot rewrite.
Years you wish you could recover.
But this is the breathtaking scandal of grace:
Jesus Christ specializes in meeting sinners inside stories they cannot repair by themselves.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
And sometimes the first sentence of a redeemed marriage sounds nothing like a sermon.
Sometimes it is simply a husband standing before the woman he wounded, with no excuses left, whispering:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me. Jesus, teach me how to love her.”
Because the strongest husband in the room may not be the man who never bends.
It may be the man finally humble enough to kneel before Christ.
The Gospel does not merely change where a man will spend eternity—it changes how he treats the woman sitting beside him tonight.
